segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Where do wars come from, and where do fights among you come from? Is it not from this: your pleasures, which are on campaign in the parts of your body?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You desire and do not have; you murder and covet and cannot obtain; you fight and wage war. You do not have because you do not ask.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? So whoever chooses to be a friend of the world is made an enemy of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or do you think the scripture speaks to no purpose when it says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The spirit he made to dwell in us yearns enviously”?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he gives greater grace. Therefore it says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “God opposes the arrogant, but to the humble he gives grace.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So submit to God. But resist the devil, and he will flee from you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will lift you up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not speak against one another, brothers and sisters. Whoever speaks against a brother or sister, or judges them, speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There is one lawgiver and judge, the one who is able to save and to destroy. But you, who are you to judge your neighbor?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Come now, you who say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Today or tomorrow we will travel to such-and-such a city and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: you who do not know what tomorrow holds or what your life will be! For you are a mist that appears for a little while and then disappears.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Instead, you ought to say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If the Lord wills, we will both live and do this or that.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But as it is, you boast in your pretensions. All such boasting is evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So whoever knows the good they ought to do and does not do it, for that person it is sin.

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for pleasure or enjoyment (the root of 'hedonism'), not a word for desire. Most English versions render it 'passions' or 'desires' because James pictures the pleasures as a driving force. 'Pleasures' is kept here and in verse 3 so the reader sees the same word both times: the pursuit of enjoyment is what is at war within them.

notes.phrase: you murder and covet and cannot obtain
notes.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and the sentence can be divided differently: 'You desire and do not have, so you murder; you covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and wage war.' The translation follows the punctuation of the SBLGNT. 'Murder' is startling in a letter to congregations, and some scholars take it as hyperbole or as the end point of unchecked desire. A long-standing conjecture reads 'you envy' instead, but no manuscript supports it.

notes.traditional: You adulterous people / Ye adulterers and adulteresses
notes.note: The Greek is a feminine plural, literally 'adulteresses'. James is drawing on the prophets' picture of God's people as an unfaithful wife (as in Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel); he is not singling out women or speaking of sexual sin. Most modern versions paraphrase as 'adulterous people'. Later manuscripts added 'adulterers and', which is the source of the King James wording.

notes.phrase: “The spirit he made to dwell in us yearns enviously”?
notes.traditional: He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us
notes.note: This is one of the most disputed sentences in the letter. 'The spirit' can be either subject or object. Many modern versions take God as the subject, jealously longing for the spirit he placed in us, which suits the image of the unfaithful wife in verse 4. The reading chosen here takes the human spirit as the subject, because the word for envy (phthonos) is always a vice in Greek usage and is not otherwise used of God's jealousy. On this reading verse 6 answers the problem: God gives a grace greater than that envy.

No passage in the Hebrew Bible or its Greek translation matches these words. James may be summarizing the general teaching of Scripture, citing a writing now lost, or, as some propose, the question about Scripture may end before the quoted words and point ahead to the proverb in verse 6. The matter is unresolved.

The quotation is Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form. The traditional 'the proud' is accurate, but in modern English 'proud' is often a compliment. The Greek word is always negative and describes people who hold themselves above others, so 'arrogant' is used.

notes.phrase: what tomorrow holds or what your life will be
notes.note: The Greek is compressed and the manuscripts differ in small ways here. It can also be read as a single clause, 'you do not know what your life will be like tomorrow', or with a separate question, 'What is your life?', as in many versions. The sense is the same on all three readings: the planners cannot see even one day ahead.

The word describes the manner of the braggart who claims more than he has or can deliver. Here it is the confident assumption that one controls the future. Most versions use 'arrogance'. 'Pretensions' keeps the idea of empty claims and stays distinct from the different Greek word translated 'arrogant' in verse 6.

candidates.rendering: brothers and sisters (plural address); brother or sister (singular, generic)
candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the letters as an address to mixed congregations, and translators divide between 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' and 'believers', so one policy is needed for plural and for generic singular uses.
A central term across the New Testament where 'grace', 'favor' and 'gift' are all defensible, and variation would hide the continuity from readers.
Frequent in Paul in both negative and positive senses ('boast', 'glory', 'take pride'), and needs one decision together with its nouns καύχησις and καύχημα.
The adjective and its verb ταπεινόω recur across the Gospels and letters with a range from 'humble' to 'lowly' or 'humiliated', and the link between them should stay visible.
Used across John, Paul and James in senses from the created universe to human society opposed to God, and readers benefit from a consistent policy on when 'world' is kept.
